'''''Trifolium campestre''''', commonly known as '''hop trefoil''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''field clover'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRCA5|taxon=Trifolium campestre|access-date=15 December 2015}}</ref> and '''low hop clover''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] native to Europe and western Asia.

==Description==
[[File:Trifolium campestre - Flickr - Kevin Thiele.jpg|thumb|upright|Leaves and flower]]

It is a herbaceous [[annual plant]], growing to {{convert|10–30|cm|frac=2}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate and trifoliate, with three oblong or elliptical leaflets {{Convert|4–10|mm|frac=4}} long.

The distinctive yellow [[flowerheads]] superficially resemble [[hops|hop]] flowers. Each flowerhead is a cylindrical or spherical collection of 20–40 individual [[flower]]s. The flowers turn brown with age and drying, enclosing the fruit, a single-seeded pod.

=== Similar plants ===
The species may be confused with others that have three leaflets and small yellow flowers, such as [[Trifolium aureum|''T. aureum'']] (large hop trefoil), [[Trifolium dubium|''T. dubium'']] (lesser hop trefoil), ''[[Medicago lupulina]]'' (black medick), and ''[[Oxalis stricta]]'' (yellow woodsorrel).

== Etymology ==
The species name ''campestre'' means "of the fields".

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Flower6.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]]]]

It is native to Europe and western Asia, growing in dry, sandy [[grassland]] habitats, fields, woodland margins, roadsides, wastelands and cultivated land.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}

It has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in [[North America]], particularly in the west and south of the continent.

== Uses ==

Hop trefoil is an important clover in [[agriculture]] because its foliage is good for feeding [[livestock]] and replenishing [[soil]]. It is not generally planted, but is considered a valuable [[herb]] when found growing in a pasture.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}
